حکایت‌های ۱–۴۱

حکایت شمارهٔ ۱

I heard of a king who gave the order to put a prisoner to death.

The poor wretch, in that state of despair, began cursing the king and speaking abusively—for it has been said: whoever gives up on his life says whatever is in his heart.

The open-ended construction «هر که / هر چه» means “whoever / whatever.” It presents a general possibility rather than one identified event, helping explain the subjunctive forms بشوید and بگوید.

When, in a desperate moment, no escape remains, a man will grasp the edge of the sharp sword.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نَمانَد and بگیرَد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

When a man despairs, his tongue grows long—like a defeated cat that attacks a dog.

Saadi switches from Persian into an Arabic quotation here. Its endings belong to Arabic case and agreement, so they should not be analyzed as Persian ezāfe or Persian personal endings.

The king asked, “What is he saying?” One good-natured minister said, “My lord! He is saying: ‘those who restrain their anger and pardon other people.’”

Saadi switches from Persian into an Arabic quotation here. Its endings belong to Arabic case and agreement, so they should not be analyzed as Persian ezāfe or Persian personal endings.

The king was moved to mercy and spared his life.

Another minister, who was the first minister’s adversary, said: “It does not befit men of our kind to speak anything but the truth in the presence of kings. This man insulted the king and spoke abusively.”

The king frowned at these words and said: “His lie pleased me more than this truth you spoke: the intention of the former was beneficial, while the foundation of the latter was malice.”

The compact form زین is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

The wise have said: “A conciliatory lie is better than a troublemaking truth.” Whoever has the king do what he says ought surely to speak nothing but good.

The open-ended construction «هر که / هر چه» means “whoever / whatever.” It presents a general possibility rather than one identified event, helping explain the subjunctive forms کُنَد and گوید and باشد and گوید.

It was written upon the arch of Fereydun’s palace: O brother, the world remains for no one; fasten your heart upon the Creator of the world, and that is enough.

This is a compound verbal construction: نِبِشته supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

Do not rely upon worldly dominion and family line: it has raised and killed many like you. When the pure soul resolves to depart, what difference is there between dying on a throne and dying upon the earth?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive کُنَد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۲

One of the kings of Khorasan saw Mahmud of Ghazni in a dream in such a state that his whole body had crumbled and become earth, except for his eyes, which still moved about in their sockets and kept looking.

This is a compound verbal construction: ریخته and شده supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

The other sages were unable to interpret this, except for a dervish who understood it and said: “He is still anxious because his kingdom is in the hands of others.”

Many a renowned man they have buried beneath the earth, of whose existence no trace remained upon its surface.

The compact form کز is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

And that old corpse whom they committed beneath the clay—the earth consumed him so completely that not a bone remained of him.

The compact form وآن and کزو is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

The blessed name of Nushirvan lives on in goodness, although a very long time has passed since Nushirvan ceased to be.

Do some good, O so-and-so, and count life as a precious opportunity—before the cry goes up: “So-and-so is no more.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive برآید; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۳

I heard of a prince who was short and slight, while his other brothers were tall and handsome. Once, his father looked at him with aversion and contempt.

This is a compound verbal construction: کوتاه supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

The son perceived this through his intelligence and insight and said: “Father, a short wise man is better than a tall fool; not everything greater in stature is greater in worth.”

The sheep is clean, while the elephant is carrion. Sinai is the smallest of the earth’s mountains, yet before God it is the greatest in worth and rank.

Saadi switches from Persian into an Arabic quotation here. Its endings belong to Arabic case and agreement, so they should not be analyzed as Persian ezāfe or Persian personal endings.

Have you heard how a thin, learned man once said to a fat fool: “Even if an Arabian horse is weak, it is still better than a whole stable of donkeys.”

The compact form وگر is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

The father laughed, the pillars of state approved, and the brothers were deeply offended.

Until a man has spoken, his faults and merits remain hidden. Do not suppose every patch of brush to be empty; a leopard may be sleeping there.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive باشد and باشد and باشد and باشد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

I heard that around that time a formidable enemy appeared against the king. When the armies on both sides faced one another, this son was the first person to enter the field.

He said: “I am not the man whose back you will see on the day of battle; I am the one whose head you may see amid dust and blood. He who makes war gambles with his own blood on the field; but he who flees gambles with the blood of an army.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive باشم and بینی and بینی and آرد and بگریزد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Having said this, he charged the enemy army and struck down several fighting men. When he came before his father, he kissed the ground in homage and said:

“You to whom my person appeared insignificant: do not mistake bulk for ability. On the day of battle a lean-waisted horse is useful, not a fattened ox.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نپنداری and آید; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

It is related that the enemy army was numerous and these men were few. A group prepared to flee. The son shouted: “Men, fight—or put on women’s clothing!”

The coordinated forms بکوشید and بپوشید are direct commands; their endings and any initial بـ or negative مـ/نـ distinguish commands from statements.

His words increased the horsemen’s courage, and they attacked all at once. I heard that they defeated the enemy that very day.

The king kissed his head and eyes, embraced him, and favored him more each day until he made him his heir.

The brothers grew envious and put poison in his food. His sister saw from an upper room and slammed the little window shut. The son understood, drew his hand away from the food, and said: “It is impossible that men of merit should die and the meritless take their place.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive بمیرند and بگیرند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

No one will come beneath the owl’s shadow, even if the royal homa-bird should vanish from the world.

The compact form ور is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

The father was informed of the affair. He summoned the brothers and punished them as they deserved. Then he assigned each a portion in a different region, so that the discord subsided and the quarrel ceased; for ten dervishes can sleep under one blanket, while two kings cannot fit within one realm.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive بخسبند and نگنجند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

If a man of God eats half a loaf, he gives the other half to dervishes. A king may possess the dominion of one realm and still remain intent upon another.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۴

A band of Arab robbers had settled atop a mountain and blocked the caravan route. The inhabitants of the towns were terrified by their schemes and the sultan’s army was defeated, because they had seized an impregnable refuge on the mountain summit and made it their shelter and dwelling.

This is a compound verbal construction: نشسته and بسته and گرفته and ساخته supply the past participle, while بودند and بودند supply the tense and agreement.

The administrators of the surrounding realms were consulting about how to repel the harm they caused, saying that if the band continued in this manner for some time, resistance would become impossible.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نمایند and گردد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

A tree that has only now taken root can be pulled from its place by one person’s strength; but if you leave it so for a time, you will not tear it out by the roots even with a windlass.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive برآید and هِلی and برنگسلی; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

A spring can be stopped with a spade; once it has filled, it cannot be crossed even with an elephant.

It was resolved that they appoint someone to spy on them and wait for an opportunity, until a time when the robbers had raided a people and their station was left empty.

This is a compound verbal construction: رانده and مانده supply the past participle, while بودند supply the tense and agreement.

They sent several battle-tested, experienced men, who concealed themselves in a ravine of the mountain.

At nightfall the robbers returned, weary from travel and carrying plunder. They removed their weapons, set down their baggage and spoils, and the first enemy to attack them was sleep.

When a watch of the night had passed: the disk of the sun entered darkness; Jonah entered the mouth of the fish.

The valiant men sprang from ambush, bound each robber’s hands behind his shoulders one by one, and brought them before the king in the morning. He ordered them all put to death.

It happened that among them was a youth: the fruit of his early youth had only just ripened, and the down upon the rose-garden of his cheek had only just sprouted.

One minister kissed the foot of the king’s throne, laid the face of intercession upon the ground, and said: “This boy has not yet enjoyed the fruit of life’s garden or benefited from the prime of youth. This servant hopes that Your Majesty, in generosity and noble character, will favor me by sparing his blood.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نهد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The king frowned at these words; they did not accord with his lofty judgment, and he said: “Whoever has a bad foundation will not receive the radiance of the good. Educating the unworthy is like placing a walnut upon a dome.”

The open-ended construction «هر که / هر چه» means “whoever / whatever.” It presents a general possibility rather than one identified event, helping explain the subjunctive forms نگیرد.

“It is better to cut off this corrupt breed and uproot their lineage; extinguishing a fire while leaving an ember, or killing a viper while preserving its young, is not the work of wise men.”

Even if a cloud rains the water of life, you will never eat fruit from a willow branch. Do not spend your days with the base, for you will not obtain sugar from the reed used for matting.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive بارد and نخوری and نخوری; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The minister heard this and approved it, willingly or unwillingly; he praised the excellence of the king’s judgment and said: “What His Majesty—may his kingdom endure—has said is pure truth: if the boy had been raised among those wicked men, he would have acquired their nature and become one of them.

But I hope that in the company of good men he will accept their training and acquire the character of the wise, for he is still a child and the disposition of rebellion and hostility has not become firmly established in him. The tradition says: ‘Every child is born according to the natural disposition; then his parents make him a Jew, a Christian, or a Magian.’”

Saadi switches from Persian into an Arabic quotation here. Its endings belong to Arabic case and agreement, so they should not be analyzed as Persian ezāfe or Persian personal endings.

Lot’s wife befriended the wicked, and her prophetic household was lost. The dog of the Companions of the Cave followed the good for a few days and became as a human being.

He said this, and a group of the king’s courtiers joined him in intercession, until the king spared the youth’s life and said: “I have pardoned him, though I did not consider it wise.”

Do you know what Zal said to valiant Rostam? An enemy cannot be counted insignificant and helpless. We have often seen the water of a small spring grow until it carried away camel and load.

In short, they raised the boy in comfort and luxury and appointed teachers to educate him, until they taught him elegant speech, apt replies, and the etiquette of serving kings; he became pleasing in everyone’s eyes.

Once the minister was describing some of the boy’s qualities before the king, saying that the training of wise men had affected him and removed his former ignorance from his nature. The king smiled and said: “In the end a wolf’s cub becomes a wolf, even if it grows up among human beings.”

This is a compound verbal construction: کرده and برده supply the past participle, while است supply the tense and agreement.

A year or two passed. A band of neighborhood ruffians joined him and made a pact; when the opportunity came, he killed the minister and both his sons, carried off immeasurable wealth, took his father’s place in the robbers’ cave, and rebelled.

The king began biting the hand of astonishment with his teeth and said: “How can anyone make a fine sword from bad iron? An ignoble man does not become somebody through education, O sage.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive کند and نشود; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Rain, whose gentle nature never varies, produces tulips in a garden and weeds in salt ground. Salty earth will not produce hyacinths: do not waste seed and labor upon it. Doing good to the wicked is like doing evil to good men.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive برنیارد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۵

At the gate of Ogholmish’s palace I saw the son of an army officer who possessed indescribable intelligence, cleverness, understanding, and discernment. Signs of greatness were visible on his brow from childhood.

Above his head, through his intelligence, a star of high fortune shone.

In short, he found favor in the sultan’s eyes because he possessed beauty of both outward form and inward meaning. The wise have said: “Wealth lies in merit, not money; greatness in intelligence, not age.”

His peers envied his position, accused him of treachery, and made a futile effort to have him killed.

What blow can an enemy strike when the friend is loving?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive زند and باشد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The king asked, “What causes these people’s hostility toward you?” He replied: “In the shelter of Your Majesty’s fortune—may his kingdom endure—I have satisfied everyone except the envious man, who is satisfied only by the loss of my prosperity. May Your Majesty’s fortune and sovereignty endure.”

I am able not to hurt anyone’s feelings; but what can I do about the envious man, who suffers from himself?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نیازارم and کنم; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Die, so that you may escape, O envious man—for this is an affliction from whose suffering one cannot be freed except through death.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive برهی; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The unfortunate desire the loss of the fortunate people’s prosperity and rank.

If the bat’s eye cannot see by day, what fault is that of the fountain of sunlight?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نبیند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

If you want the truth, it is better for a thousand such eyes to be blind than for the sun to be dark.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۶

They tell of a Persian king who had stretched out the hand of aggression against his subjects’ property and begun oppression and abuse, until the people scattered through the world to escape his schemes and took the road of exile because of the anguish of his tyranny.

This is a compound verbal construction: کرده and کرده supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

When the population diminished, the province’s revenue declined, the treasury remained empty, and the enemies gained strength.

Whoever wants a rescuer on the day of disaster—tell him to practice generosity in times of safety. If you do not cherish a ring-eared servant, he will leave; show kindness, kindness, and even a stranger will become your devoted servant.

The open-ended construction «هر که / هر چه» means “whoever / whatever.” It presents a general possibility rather than one identified event, helping explain the subjunctive forms ننوازی and برود and شود.

Once, in his assembly, they were reading from the Shahnameh about the fall of Zahhak’s kingdom and the reign of Fereydun. The minister asked the king: “Can one know how sovereignty was established for Fereydun, though he possessed neither treasure, dominion, nor retinue?”

He replied: “As you heard, a people rallied around him with devotion, strengthened him, and he attained kingship.”

The minister said: “O king, since a people’s gathering together is the cause of kingship, why do you scatter the people? Can it be that you have no desire to rule?”

It is better to cherish the army as your own life, for a sultan exercises sovereignty through his army.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive پروری and کند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The king asked: “What causes the army and subjects to gather?” The minister replied: “A king must have generosity so that they gather around him, and mercy so that they may sit secure under the protection of his rule. You possess neither.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive باشد and آیند and نشینند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

One who practices oppression cannot rule, just as shepherding cannot come from a wolf. A king who lays the foundation of tyranny digs out the foot of the wall of his own kingdom.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نکند and نیاید and افکند and بکند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The sincere minister’s advice did not suit the contrary-minded king’s temperament. He frowned at these words and sent the minister to prison.

Not much time passed before the sultan’s paternal cousins rose in contention and claimed their fathers’ kingdom. People whom his aggression had driven to desperation and scattered rallied around them and strengthened them, until the kingdom passed out of this man’s control and was established for the others.

This is a compound verbal construction: آمده and شده supply the past participle, while بودند supply the tense and agreement.

A king who permits oppression of his subjects will find his supporters powerful enemies on the day of hardship. Make peace with your people and sit secure from an enemy’s attack, for the just emperor’s people are his army.

The coordinated forms کن and نشین are direct commands; their endings and any initial بـ or negative مـ/نـ distinguish commands from statements.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۷

A king boarded a ship with a Persian slave. The slave had never seen the sea or experienced the hardship of sailing. He began weeping and lamenting, and trembling seized his body. However much they soothed him, he would not calm down, and the king’s pleasure was spoiled by him.

This is a compound verbal construction: ندیده and نیازموده supply the past participle, while بود and بود supply the tense and agreement.

They knew no remedy. A sage was on the ship and said to the king: “If you give the order, I shall quiet him by a certain method.” The king replied: “That would be the height of kindness and generosity.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive دهی and گردانم and باشد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

He ordered them to throw the slave into the sea. He went under several times; they seized him by the hair and brought him alongside the ship. He clung to the ship’s rudder with both hands.

When he came aboard, he sat in a corner and became calm. The king was astonished and asked: “What was the wisdom in this?”

The sage replied: “At first he had never tasted the hardship of drowning and did not know the value of safety aboard ship. Likewise, the value of well-being is known by someone who falls into misfortune.”

This is a compound verbal construction: ناچشیده supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

O well-fed man, barley bread does not seem pleasant to you. The one who is ugly in your eyes is my beloved.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive ننماید; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

For the houris of paradise, Purgatory would be hell; ask the inhabitants of hell, for whom Purgatory is heaven.

There is a difference between one whose beloved is in his arms and one whose two expectant eyes are fixed upon the door.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۸

They asked Hormoz: “What offense did you find in your father’s ministers that you ordered them imprisoned?”

He replied: “I discovered no definite offense, but I saw that their fear of me was boundless and that they had no complete confidence in my reign.

I feared that, from anxiety about harm to themselves, they might plan my destruction. I therefore acted upon the sages’ saying:

Fear the person who fears you, O sage, even if you could face a hundred like him in battle.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive ترسد and برآیی; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The snake strikes the shepherd’s foot because it fears that he will crush its head with a stone.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive زند and ترسد and بکوبد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Do you not see that when a cat becomes desperate, it will tear out a leopard’s eye with its claws?”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نبینی and شود and برآرد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۹

An Arab king was ill in old age and had given up hope of life, when a horseman entered through the door and announced: “Through Your Majesty’s good fortune we have taken such-and-such a fortress; the enemy have been captured, and the army and population of that region have become entirely obedient to your command.”

This is a compound verbal construction: کرده supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

The king let out a cold sigh and said: “These glad tidings are not for me; they are for my enemies”—meaning the heirs to his kingdom.

Alas, my precious life came to an end in the hope that what is in my heart would come to me through my door.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive آید; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The hope I cherished was fulfilled, but what use is it, since there is no hope that a life already passed will return?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive بازآید; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

The hand of fate has struck the drum of departure. O my two eyes, bid farewell to my head; O palm, forearm, and upper arm, all bid farewell to one another.

The coordinated forms بکنید and بکنید are direct commands; their endings and any initial بـ or negative مـ/نـ distinguish commands from statements.

The enemy who obtains his desire has fallen upon me. At last, friends, pass by me. My life went by in ignorance; I did not take care—do you take warning.

The coordinated forms بکنید and بکنید are direct commands; their endings and any initial بـ or negative مـ/نـ distinguish commands from statements.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۱۰

I was in devotional retreat beside the tomb of the prophet John—peace be upon him—in the Great Mosque of Damascus, when an Arab king, known for injustice, happened to come on pilgrimage, prayed, supplicated, and asked for his need.

Dervish and rich man are servants at this dusty door; and those who are richer are more needy.

Then he said to me: “By the spiritual resolve of dervishes and the sincerity of their dealings, direct a favorable thought toward me, for I am apprehensive of a formidable enemy.”

I told him: “Show mercy to your weak subjects, so that you suffer no trouble from a powerful enemy.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نبینی; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

With powerful arms and the strength of your wrist, it is wrong to break the hand of the helpless poor.

Should the one who shows no mercy to the fallen not fear that, if he himself is brought down, no one will take his hand?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نترسد and نبخشاید and درآید and نگیرد; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Whoever sows the seed of evil while expecting goodness has nursed a vain fancy and formed a false hope.

Take the cotton from your ear and give the people justice; and if you do not give justice, there is a Day of Judgment.

The compact form وگر is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

The children of Adam are limbs of one another, created from a single essence. When fate brings one limb to pain, the other limbs cannot remain at ease.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive آورد and نماند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

You who are unconcerned by the suffering of others do not deserve to be called human.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نهند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۱۱

A dervish whose prayers were answered appeared in Baghdad. They informed Hajjaj ibn Yusuf. He summoned the dervish and said: “Offer a good prayer for me.”

The dervish said: “O God, take his life!” Hajjaj said: “For God’s sake, what sort of prayer is this?” He replied: “This is a good prayer for you and for all Muslims.”

O powerful oppressor of the weak, how long will this flourishing trade continue?

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive بماند; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

Of what use is world-rule to you? Your dying is better than your tormenting people.

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive آیدت; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۱۲

An unjust king asked a pious man: “Which act of worship is most excellent?” He replied: “For you, a midday sleep—so that during it you do not harm the people for even one breath.”

The subordinate or non-asserted setting introduced in this sentence helps license the subjunctive نیازاری; these actions are presented as possible, intended, general, or dependent rather than as simple completed facts.

I saw an oppressor sleeping at midday and said: “This man is a source of strife; it is better that sleep has carried him away.”

This is a compound verbal construction: خفته and برده supply the past participle, while فتنه‌ست supply the tense and agreement.

The one whose sleep is better than his wakefulness has lived so wickedly that he is better dead.

This is a compound verbal construction: مرده supply the past participle, while بیداری‌ست supply the tense and agreement.

حکایت شمارهٔ ۱۳

I heard of a king who had passed a night in revelry and, at the end of his drunkenness, kept saying:

This is a compound verbal construction: کرده supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

For us there is no moment in the world pleasanter than this one: there is no thought of good or evil, and no concern about anyone.

The compact form کز is a classical or poetic contraction. Expanding it into its component words makes the sentence structure easier to see.

A dervish was sleeping outside in the cold and said: “O you whose good fortune has no equal in the world: grant that you have no sorrow—but have you no concern for us either?”

This is a compound verbal construction: خفته supply the past participle, while بود supply the tense and agreement.

The king was pleased. He held a purse of a thousand dinars out through the window and said: “Hold out your skirt, dervish.”
